questions.q: What is the rule's actual configured source range, versus the vendor's documented range?
options: Both are 198.51.100.16/28 -- there is no mismatch
The rule is configured as 198.51.0.0/16; the vendor's documented range is 198.51.100.16/28
The rule is configured as 198.51.100.16/28; the vendor's documented range is 198.51.0.0/16
Neither range was ever documented
questions.explain: The rule was written far wider (a /16) than the vendor's actual contracted range (a /28).

questions.q: How many addresses does 198.51.100.16/28 cover, versus 198.51.0.0/16?
options: 16 addresses versus 65,536 addresses
256 addresses versus 65,536 addresses
16 addresses versus 256 addresses
They cover the same number of addresses
questions.explain: A /28 covers 16 addresses; a /16 covers 65,536 -- a massive difference in exposed address space.

questions.q: Why did nobody notice this mismatch for ongoing operations?
options: The vendor's real range sits entirely inside the configured /16, so the vendor's legitimate traffic always worked and nothing looked broken
The firewall logged an error every time the vendor connected
The rule was reviewed monthly and always passed
The vendor never actually used the rule
questions.explain: Because the vendor's /28 is a subset of the configured /16, day-to-day operation never surfaced the mistake.

questions.q: What does the rule's change history show?
options: It was edited the night before the 3 AM alert
It was created during Lesson 4's deadline-pressured setup and never revisited since
It was created by the vendor directly
It has no creation date on record
questions.explain: The rule has existed unreviewed since the original deadline-pressured setup -- this is not a recent change.

questions.q: What is the real risk created by the /16 scope, beyond the one IP that triggered the alert?
options: None -- only that one IP could ever have connected
Any address inside the full 65,536-address range could have reached the jump host's RDP port the whole time the rule existed
The vendor's own connection was at risk of being blocked
The correlation rule from Lesson 5 would have caught any other address automatically
questions.explain: The 3 AM alert is the first noticed instance, not the first possible one -- the whole /16 was reachable the entire time.
